{{DISPLAYTITLE:{{math|''Y''}} and {{math|'''H'''}}  transforms}}
In mathematics, the {{math|''Y''}} '''transforms''' and {{math|'''H'''}} '''transforms''' are complementary pairs of [[integral transform]]s involving, respectively, the [[Neumann function]] ([[Bessel function]] of the second kind) {{math|''Y''<sub>''ν''</sub>}} of order {{math|''ν''}} and the [[Struve function]] {{math|'''H'''<sub>''ν''</sub>}} of the same order.

For a given function {{math|''f''(''r'')}}, the {{math|''Y''}}-transform of order {{math|''ν''}} is given by

:<math>F(k) = \int_0^\infty f(r) Y_{\nu}(kr) \sqrt{kr} \, dr </math>

The inverse of above is the {{math|'''H'''}}-transform of the same order; for a given function {{math|''F''(''k'')}}, the {{math|'''H'''}}-transform of order {{math|''ν''}} is given by
:<math>f(r) = \int_0^\infty F(k) \mathbf{H}_{\nu}(kr) \sqrt{kr} \, dk </math>

These transforms are closely related to the [[Hankel transform]], as both involve Bessel functions.
In problems of mathematical physics and applied mathematics, the Hankel, {{math|''Y''}}, {{math|'''H'''}} transforms all may appear in problems having [[axial symmetry]].
Hankel transforms are however much more commonly seen due to their connection with the 2-dimensional Fourier transform. The {{math|''Y''}}, {{math|'''H'''}} transforms appear in situations with singular behaviour on the axis of symmetry.{{sfn|Rooney|1980}}
<!--

Below is probably not necessary given the lack of Fourier connection...
==Alternative definition==

As with the Hankel transform, an alternative notation is available where square roots of {{math|''r''}} and {{math|''k''}} are refactored into the functions under consideration, viz:

:<math>G(k) = \int_0^\infty g(r) Y_\nu(kr) r \, dr </math>
:<math>g(r) = \int_0^\infty} G(k) \mathbf{H}_\nu(kr) k \, dk </math>

This can be compared to the previous definitions by the substitutions

:<math>g(r) = \frac{f(r)}{\sqrt{r}}, \qquad G(k) = \frac{F(k)}{\sqrt{k}}.</math>
-->
